12317-two-little-knights-of-kentucky:
Two Little Knights of Kentucky is a children book about the Little Colonel circle, dedicated to Margaret, Albion, Mary, Helen, Lura, Rose, William, and George. The story belongs to Annie Fellows Johnston Little Colonel series, set in Lloydsborough, Kentucky.

Chapters open on the coldest Saint Valentine eve Kentucky had known in twenty years, with two tramps and a bear. Later chapters bring Ginger and the boys, a valentine party, a fire and a plan, Jonesy benefit, and the Little Colonel two rescues. A mid-book scene has Virginia admire pretty articles made from almost nothing, including a helmet with nodding plumes. The book mixes play, rescue, and Southern manners for young readers.
13933-in-old-kentucky:
Edward Marshall and Charles T. Dazey turned Dazey's play In Old Kentucky into a 1910 novel of the Bluegrass and the mountains. Illustrations by Clarence Rowe picture a stranger breaking through undergrowth about a pool and a leap beyond a blazing barrier. Mountain folk, horse lovers, and Bluegrass gentry meet and clash.

A mountain girl gazes at a wondrous view and declares learning could not make her love it more. Feuds, races, and romances drive the plot, in the manner of the stage original. The novel keeps the play's broad humour and sentiment. It captures Kentucky local colour as popular audiences loved it. Readers of regional romance will enjoy its pace.
15521-the-adventures-of-prickly-porky:
Thornton W. Burgess published this bedtime story book in Boston in 1916, with Little, Brown, illustrated by Harrison Cady. It belongs to his Bedtime Story-Books, beside the Old Mother West Wind series. A frontispiece shows a cry for news of Peter Rabbit, setting the woodland cast in motion.

Twenty-three chapters follow Prickly Porky, the porcupine stranger from the north, as he makes friends, nearly chokes, and meets Jimmy Skunk, Unc' Billy Possum, Reddy Fox, and Old Granny Fox. Peter Rabbit tells his story many times, a plot frightens Old Man Coyote, and Buster Bear gives it all away. Burgess writes short, gentle chapters for young children, teaching animal lore through talk, trouble, and friendship in the Green Forest.
19477-the-young-trailers-a-story-of-earl:
Joseph A. Altsheler wrote this tale of early Kentucky, published in the early nineteen hundreds. Two boys, Henry and Paul, push into unknown woods, lose their way, explore a great cave by torchlight, and face a siege that tests their courage and their bond.

Chapters on haunted forests, giant bones, and a wild turkey's call give the frontier its wonder as well as its danger. Altsheler wrote many such books for boys, and this one shows his formula at its best: young heroes learning woodcraft, loyalty, and duty on the edge of settlement.
20649-oomphel-in-the-sky:
H. Beam Piper's Oomphel in the Sky is a science fiction story set on a colony world far from Earth. It opens with a communication screen snapping on. Harry Walsh, the news editor, looks out from his office in Bluelake, halfway across the continent, and wants to know how things are going.

The man he calls is deep in trouble with the planet's native peoples. Their word oomphel names the strange sky craft and goods they cannot explain. Piper, famous for his future histories, builds the tale on language, trade, and the clash of two worlds' ideas.
20719-under-the-country-sky:
Grace S. Richmond set her novel Under the Country Sky in a country town, among the people her heroine serves and loves. Richmond wrote warm stories of doctors, ministers, and their families in small places. Her heroine's patience with her neighbors is tested on every page.

She loved them all, the narrator explains, so it would go hard with her if she had to hate them. Love turned to hate is such a bitter product. But she had never found it so hard to be patient with them as now. Under that strain, the novel tests what small-town kindness costs the one who gives it.
21568-sweet-their-blood-and-sticky:
Albert R. Teichner's tale Sweet Their Blood and Sticky ran in Worlds of If in November 1961. A vast machine, hundreds of feet long, stands working alone in a desert. It can run on a thimbleful of earth or water, drawing all it needs from the land.

With its packing gear broken, the machine pours out a stream of pink-striped taffy. Once a whole desert of such devices fed a needful human race. Now the makers are gone, and something not human inherits the earth. Teichner builds a chill, strange tale from candy, dust, and four dimensions.
23327-lodusky:
Frances Hodgson Burnett set this tale among mountain folk in Tennessee in eighteen seventy seven. Lodusky, a slight young woman who earns her keep by writing, comes to a rough country dance with an older kinswoman, and the local folk eye the pair with keen interest.

The story moves through dances, games, and talk at mountain homes, where manners are plain and speech is blunt. Lodusky watches it all with bright eyes, while neighbours weigh her book learning against their own ways. Burnett uses the gap between the visiting writer and her hosts to draw a warm, close picture of mountain life and of a young woman finding her place in it.
23798-daniel-boone-the-pioneer-of-kentuc:
John S. C. Abbott published Daniel Boone, The Pioneer of Kentucky, in 1872, in the American Pioneers and Patriots series. Abbott opens by challenging the popular image of Boone as a crude frontiersman, nearly as wild as the bears he hunted and the Native peoples he confronted.

Abbott presents the opposite portrait instead: a mild man who never boasted, gentle in taste and bearing, who kept coarse speech and rude conduct out of his life. With that refinement went a boldness that seemed incapable of fear. Abbott's life follows Boone's wonderful career for young readers, presenting him as nature's gentleman on the frontier.
23882-gold-in-the-sky:
Alan E. Nourse published Gold in the Sky as a book-length novel in Amazing Science Fiction Stories in September 1958. Its cast is introduced at once. Greg Hunter is a test pilot happy only when his life hangs in the balance. Tom Hunter is a pioneer whose frontier hides in test tubes. Johnny Coombs is a prospector who returned from the asteroids too soon.

Against them stand Merrill Tawney, an industrialist seeking plunder beyond the stars, and Major Briarton, a government man whose creed is law and order. Chapters run from Trouble Times Two and Jupiter Equilateral through the Black Raider, the Haunted Ship, and the Sinister Bonanza to the Missing Asteroid and the Final Move. It is space adventure with gold at its heart.
24558-watch-the-sky:
James H. Schmitz wrote this short science-fiction story, illustrated by Hortens. Its opening warns that getting caught in a lie is one thing, and finding the lie is not a lie is far worse. The story's strange object is a Geest gun, battered by war and pulled out of shape, that belonged to Uncle William Boles.

Its scarred twin barrels are stubby and thick, and its curved stock, too thin and knobbed to fit a human hand, marks it as alien work. Schmitz builds his tale around that gun and what it implies. Readers get a sharp, compact story of alien weapons, old soldiers, and a truth nobody expected.
26728-aunt-jane-of-kentucky:
Eliza Calvert Hall, author of The Land of Long Ago, published these Kentucky sketches with A. L. Burt Company at New York, with frontispiece and page decorations by Beulah Strong. Copyrights run from 1898 to 1907. Hall's epigraph from Maeterlinck promises that emotion in an old-fashioned country parlor can stir the heart as mightily as a king's majestic passion.

Aunt Jane receives her visitor in June in Kentucky, with clover and blue-grass running sweet riot across the road and clover odors blowing through a white-curtained window. Her room holds a hit-or-miss rag carpet, Shaker rockers with shuck bottoms, and a shining mahogany table. She wears purple calico, a gingham apron with a capacious pocket, and a substantial black lace cap tied under her chin. Chapters include Sally Ann's experience, the new organ, Aunt Jane's album, and the baptizing at Kittle Creek.
2803-the-rise-of-david-levinsky:
Abraham Cahan wrote The Rise of David Levinsky as the life story of a Jewish immigrant who climbs from poverty to wealth in New York's garment trade. Levinsky arrives as a Talmud student from Russia, works his way through sweatshops and peddling, and slowly learns the business of cloaks and suits. The novel follows his rise alongside his hunger for learning, love, and respect.

Cahan sets Levinsky's success against what it costs him, since business skill never quite fills the place left by faith and feeling. Scenes of the Lower East Side, the shops, and the counting houses give the story its texture. It endures as an immigrant novel that refuses to treat wealth as a simple happy ending.
28239-the-story-of-kentucky:
R. S. Eubank wrote The Story of Kentucky in 1913 for the Instructor Literature Series, published at Dansville, New York. Eubank traces Kentucky from its geography and first white visitors, through Virginians and Daniel Boone, to settlements, pioneer life, and George Rogers Clark in the Revolution. Later chapters cover schools, state government, Indian wars, and the War of 1812.

The book also treats internal improvements, slavery, and the Civil War, in short, clear chapters for school readers. Eubank stresses the Blue Grass country, the Pennyrile, and the mountain east. The volume offers a compact, old-fashioned school history of Kentucky.
29133-shipwreck-in-the-sky:
Eando Binder wrote this science fiction tale about a famous flight into space. Pilot-Captain Dan Barstow was chosen for Project Songbird. The Space Medicine Labs of the United States Air Force backed the project. Barstow flew the VX-3, a craft that had already broken records set by V-2 rockets and Navy Aerobees. He became the first pilot to cross the sea of air and glimpse open space.

Binder, welcomed back by the magazine as a legend of the genre, tells the flight as a folktale of the future. Barstow settles in for the long jaunt, watching thirty-seven instruments, too busy to feel thrilled or scared. Readers get a compact space-pioneer story, heroic in tone, about a record flight that turns into a shipwreck in the sky.
32473-the-buttoned-sky:
Geoff St. Reynard's tale, printed in Imagination in August 1953, is set in a future ruled by god-globes, where men gaze fearfully at a buttoned sky. Legends recall a glorious free past for Earth, but the present belongs to priests, squires, and globes that sap power. A ballad quoted at the opening has a squire in Dolfya Town drinking blood-dark wine. He asks who can blight his happiness, while his daughter warns that priest, globe, and Mink can end his joy.

The story's hero, Revel, wakes early on the day he kills a god, with a bitter taste and a pain in his ear from a shebeen brawl. His bed is a hollow in an earth floor filled with leaves and mink skins sewn into a blanket. From that rough morning, Reynard builds a tale of rebellion against godlike machines and the men who serve them.
35491-boris-lensky:
Boris Lensky is a novel by Ossip Schubin, the pen name of Lola Kirschner, translated from the German by Elise Lathrop. Worthington printed it in New York in 1891. A Carlyle line heads the tale: the hero had many faults, but not the fault of quackery.

A concert notice opens the book, urging readers to see what power the charm of music holds over humanity. In Russia they call Lensky the devil's violinist. The tale told of him says a poor Moscow child scraped his violin for scant food as a boy. He refused the devil his soul but accepted a gift: a charm in his art that no one could resist. He wanders the world restless and joyless under the curse of that gift.
36047-the-red-debt-echoes-from-kentucky:
Everett Macdonald published The Red Debt with Dillingham of New York in April 1916. The subtitle calls the novel echoes from Kentucky. William Oberhardt drew the illustrations from original drawings.

Macdonald writes a Kentucky novel of his own time. The title's red debt suggests a blood reckoning carried on the books of a family or a county. Kentucky fiction of the period ran on feuds, honor, and the long memory of the mountains. Dillingham built a list on such regional novels, sold to readers who wanted their own counties in print. The Red Debt belongs to the last flourishing of that trade, just before the war changed American fiction's subjects. Its Kentucky is a place where old accounts stay open until somebody pays them.
36736-molly-brown-of-kentucky:
Molly Brown of Kentucky is a novel by Nell Speed, copyright nineteen seventeen. Speed is billed as author of the Tucker Twins and Carter Girls series. The hosted text was printed in the United States and issued by a New York house. Its contents run to twenty three chapters.

Chapter heads set a story that moves between Kentucky and wartime Europe. They name an orchard home, afternoon tea, and letters from Paris and Berlin. Later heads name a Zeppelin raid, a cablegram, and a war bride. The opening text places Molly with friends at Giverny. It notes how a married pair in the group get on better than most, in a light comic tone. The mix of home scenes and war heads gives the book its shape.
37498-stories-of-old-kentucky:
Stories of Old Kentucky, by Martha Grassham Purcell, was published in 1915. Purcell, of Paducah, gives the book to her children, who had ever been her inspiring audience. She was also a member of the board of education there, and had written on Louisiana settlements.

The tales begin long before settlement, when the ocean covered Kentucky. They treat the first peoples, old remains, discovery, and Indian claims. Boone fills much of the book: his trace, his captivity, and the brave defence of Boonesborough. Other tales tell of pioneer customs, weddings in the wilds, children, lost babies, and how the pioneers made change. Readers get short Kentucky history tales for the young, from mammoth graves to the Civil War.
40487-happy-go-lucky:
Ian Hay tells a schoolboy's road in Happy-Go-Lucky, from Houghton Mifflin of Boston and New York, published in August 1913, with pictures by C E Brock. The contents divide the tale into three books: Youthful Excursions, A Blind Alley, and The Right Road. The Real Tilly and The Real Mr Welwyn wait near the end.

The tale opens at Grandwich School, where the London contingent of the Hivite House breakfasts together at the Imperial Hotel at Oakleigh before the nine-fifty-two train. Rumbold major's stiff third-person note to the landlord begs the feast at half-a-crown a head. High spirits rule from the first page.
40597-miniature-essays-igor-stravinsky:
Miniature Essays on Igor Stravinsky is a small life and work pamphlet. Chester of London and Geneva sold it for sixpence in nineteen twenty one. Agents in Paris, Brussels, Amsterdam, and Bologna stocked the Chester miniature set. A Lausanne photograph of the composer fronts the sixpenny essay here.

Stravinsky was born at Oranienbaum, near Saint Petersburg, in June eighteen eighty two. His father sang opera at the Maryinsky Theatre in the Russian capital. The father soon found rare musical gifts in the growing boy at home. The essay traces his rise in brief for concert goers of the day. Chester miniature essays gave short composer lives at a low price.
41673-nullification-secession-webster-s-:
Nullification, Secession, Webster's Argument, and the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions is a constitutional study by Caleb William Loring, published by Putnam's Sons in 1893. Loring says he was shocked to read, in a Life of Webster, that Hayne really had the right of the argument in the great nullification debate. In reply he prepared a statement of Webster's argument, set against the text of the Constitution itself.

The vital question, as he frames it, is what the states made in 1787. Did they establish a national union, or a confederacy of separate nations, each free to judge federal acts and leave at pleasure? Loring argues the Constitution itself proves a nation was founded, armed with sovereign authority. He adds that historically there was no early contention on the point.
43915-theodor-leschetizky:
Theodor Leschetizky, by Annette Hullah, is a short life of the famed piano teacher of Vienna. It belongs to the Living Masters of Music series, edited by Rosa Newmarch, and was published in London in 1906.

The first chapters trace Leschetizky's life from 1830 to 1862 and then to 1905. He was born on June 22, 1830, at the Castle of Lancut in Poland, the son of a Bohemian father. Later chapters explain how his famed method grew and what the method is. Others describe his lessons and his class of pupils at work. Photographs show the master at the piano, his villa in Vienna, and a group of his pupils. A line from Browning about striving for life's set prize stands as the motto.
45259-the-life-letters-of-peter-ilich-tc:
Modeste Tchaikovsky's The Life & Letters of Peter Ilich Tchaikovsky was edited from the Russian by Rosa Newmarch, who also wrote the introduction. John Lane issued it in London and New York in 1906. Newmarch gives the book to Sergei Ivanovich Taneiev and to all who keep the composer's memory.

The life is told in seven parts by years: 1840 to 1861, then the conservatory years, the long middle run to 1885, and the last part, 1888 to 1893. The plates track the man through them, from the house at Votinsk where he was born to a portrait of 1893. His father, his mother, and the family in 1848 all stand in the early pages.
46701-discourses-of-keidansky:
Bernard Richards wrote Discourses of Keidansky, published in New York in 1903 in a first edition of that March. A note owns that most of the papers first appeared in the Boston Evening Transcript. The editors' leave to reprint them is thanked, and all the papers have been much changed, with many fixes and additions. An opening piece sets the figure of Keidansky before the reader.

Far-out, image-breaking, and insurgent, the piece calls him; yet the flashing eye, the trembling hand, and the stirring voice held hearers spellbound. Outrageous heresies, some said, yet those who paused to listen lingered longer. These dreamers, holding forth over tea in the cafés or under the floating red flag, were but a line of the prophets of old in Israel. The papers may shed some light, the piece hopes, on the inner life of that strange world called the Ghetto.
49143-the-boy-hunters-of-kentucky:
The Boy Hunters of Kentucky is a boys' frontier novel by Edward Ellis, published by Cassell in 1889 in its sixtieth thousand. Ellis wrote many such tales, including Red Feather and Wolf Ear the Indian. An illustration shows Jack meeting a boy not much older than himself. The first chapter makes Jack a young pioneer, and the second trains him as a Kentucky rifleman.

The meeting on the bridge and the home of Jack follow. A young Wyandot appears, and a wrestling bout tests the boys. Jack resumes his journey southward, and the chapters turn to royal game. Hunting the hunters reverses the sport, and George makes a shot. A strange camp fire, captive and captors, and a signal and its reply raise the danger. A passage preserved in the copy introduces the setting through Daniel Boone.
50823-the-flying-boys-in-the-sky:
Edward Ellis begins his Flying Boys series with The Flying Boys in the Sky, published by Winston at Philadelphia with copyright in 1911. Edwin Prittie drew the pictures, and the volume sold alone or boxed with its sequel, The Flying Boys to the Rescue. Ellis was known for his Catamount Camp and Deerfoot series.

Thirty-three chapters run from Learning to Fly to a closing chapter asking where Bohunkus is. The contents promise aeroplane races, altitude trials, a working for dinner episode, and lectures from a professor on aviation. Later chapters bring a biplane destroyed, a puzzling telegram, a cabin in the woods, and shots fired by kidnappers. Search and rescue drives the back half, ending in retribution and explained mysteries.
50847-tea-tray-in-the-sky:
Tea Tray in the Sky is a science fiction story by Evelyn E Smith, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction for September 1952 with pictures by Ashman. The tale follows Michael, a young man fresh out of the Angeleno Brotherhood, where the brothers shave a tonsure into the scalp. His half-grown stubble marks him at once as a man who has left the cloister for the world.

His shelf mate on the ship asks the obvious question: why would a good-looking young fellow join a Brotherhood? Around them the future runs its adverts, pushing Grugis juice for the rundown and nervous. Smith mixes cloistered innocence with sales talk and space travel, and the comedy comes from Michael's polite inexperience among worldly passengers.
51187-a-visit-to-the-mammoth-cave-of-ken:
John Wilson, the Scottish vocalist, visited the Mammoth Cave on a singing tour of America and printed his letter at Edinburgh in 1849. The journey itself fills half the fun: a stage from Nashville, breakfast at Tyree Springs, forced suppers at Bowling Green, and a night at Bell's. Bell's Atholl brose of peach brandy and honey Wilson vows never to taste again. Eight miles of the roughest road in a four-horse stage brought the party to the cave.

Wilson counts what had been found by 1849: 226 avenues, forty-seven domes, eight cataracts, and eight rivers, only three of them explored. The cave was first discovered by the whites in 1802. In the last war with England, saltpetre was made in it in immense quantities. The utensils remain near the entrance, and the marks of the miners' oxen can still be traced in the ground.
51867-sentry-of-the-sky:
Evelyn E Smith wrote Sentry of the Sky, a tale from Galaxy Magazine in February 1961, with art by Ritter. A front note says Sub Archivist Clarey had to find a way to rise in the world. The way he finds is right out of the tri di dramas, the note jokes. Clarey goes to the Classification Center from habit more than hope.

A test machine drops a card that sends Clarey to Room 33 for a new class. Ten years past he would have felt joy at the news. Now he fears a move down, as most such moves go. He may refuse work not in his line, but the state must then keep him. The tale turns on rank, work, and pride in a future state.
52228-search-the-sky:
Search the Sky is a science fiction novel by Frederik Pohl and Kornbluth. Ballantine Books of New York issued the novel in nineteen fifty four. The tale opens on Halsey Planet, at a spaceport and its yards. A trader named Ross stands on the ramp and broods on decay.

Decay is the word that keeps rising to the top of his mind. The clean and brisk spaceport makes the sense of rot stronger still. Ghost Town, a grey tumbledown stretch, lies between port and city spires. Ross slept poorly, torn by a choice he must make that day. Readers enter a world of trade, decline, and a search to come.
56133-flowers-of-the-sky:
Flowers of the Sky is a popular astronomy book by Richard A Proctor, with fifty four pictures. Proctor is billed as author of works on the heavens, the sun, and the moon. A passage from Shelley on the spirit of nature stands at its front. Contents run to thirteen chapters, from Light and Space onward.

Later chapters treat the infinitely minute and the mystery of gravity. The end of many worlds takes a long chapter of its own. The aurora borealis and the lunar halo follow. Moonlight, Mars, Jupiter, and the ringed planet Saturn each earn a chapter. Fancied figures among the stars and transits of Venus close the list. The first chapter opens with verse on a man watching the sun rise from a headland. Light, it argues, gives assurance of one energy through all things.
5661-a-son-of-the-gods-and-a-horseman-in:
Ambrose Bierce, who fought in the Civil War as a young soldier, pairs two short studies of war in this small volume, with an introduction by Morrow. The introduction presents Bierce as poet, critic, satirist, and writer of fables, and it stresses that his war writing comes from direct experience rather than distant report. Both tales are brief, sharp, and centered on single moments when a soldier must act.

Readers get war stripped of parade and speeches, told through choice, fear, and sudden fate. The value of the pair lies in its compression. A whole argument about courage and chance rides on one watch, one ride, and one shot. The spare prose leaves the moral weight to the reader rather than spelling it out.
56870-tales-from-gorky:
Tales from Gorky gathers stories by Maxim Gorky, rendered from the Russian with a life of the author by Bain. Funk and Wagnall's published the third edition at New York in 1902. Nine tales stand in the contents. The life sketch opens by asking what chance a poor, friendless lad of weak frame and wandering bent would have, turned adrift to shift for himself at school age.

Such a boy, the sketch says, would seem bound for prison or the workhouse. But give him the spark of genius and a love of letters, and his strange road and stranger bedfellows become matchless matter. The tales include In the Steppe, Twenty-Six of Us and One Other, One Autumn Night, The Green Kitten, and Chelkash. Her Lover and Comrades stand among them.
58688-jungle-in-the-sky:
Jungle in the Sky, by Milton Lesser, first appeared in Worlds of If Science Fiction in May 1952. The hunters, its opening line says, wanted animals that lived on far Ganymede, though not as badly as the animals wanted the hunters.

The story opens in the trophy room of Brody Carmical, a famous big-game hunter whose mounted heads include a Venusian swamp-tiger and a Callistan fire-lizard. Steve Stedman, fresh out of school with a degree in extra-terrestrial zoology, begs for a job, and Carmical warns him that frontier worlds hold no Harvard clubs, beefsteak, or martinis. Stedman answers only: try me.
58995-seller-of-the-sky:
Seller of the Sky is a science fiction story by Dave Dryfoos, from Worlds of If of February 1955. A deck line presents Old Arch as an ancient, broken down wanderer seeking alms. He spreads tales of the great Outside that no adult takes seriously at all. Children, it hints, are curious and believing when adults are cynical and doubting.

Archer Jakes, the Wanderer of the Plains, was born on Earth in 3042, they say. Taken to Mazzeppa as a child, he learned pilotage and mining in his youth. A cave in injury on Hurretni in 3068 broke the man he had been. Exile, memory, and one believer frame this quiet far future tale.
59196-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
The Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Fyodor Dostoevsky is a finding volume compiled by David Widger. It gathers the tables of contents of the Dostoevsky novels and stories then available from Project Gutenberg. The list runs from Notes from the Underground and Poor Folk to the great novels of the eighteen sixties and seventies.

The contents show the translations in use: Constance Garnett for Crime and Punishment and The Possessed, Hogarth for The Gambler and Poor Folk, Eva Martin for The Idiot. Crime and Punishment fills six parts and an epilogue of numbered chapters. Poor Folk is laid out as a calendar of letters from April to September. The Possessed keeps its chapter titles, from The Subtle Serpent to Filibusters and a Fatal Morning. The index is a map of how English readers of the early ebook age first met Dostoevsky whole.
6012-charlemont-or-the-pride-of-the-vill:
W. Gilmore Simms calls Charlemont a domestic legend founded on actual events of recent occurrence in Kentucky. However strange the facts may seem, and however they clash with supposed sensibilities of woman, Simms insists most were conclusively established by the record. He dedicates the tale and its sequel Beauchampe to James Hall of Cincinnati.

The epigraph warns that security in one's own strength breeds negligence, and negligence breeds unremedied ruin. Simms, a pioneer literary voice of the West, sets village pride against private passion. The novel follows Kentucky folk whose choices turn from confidence toward trouble.
62888-masterpieces-of-adventure-stories-:
Nella Braddy edited Masterpieces of Adventure: Stories of the Sea and Sky, one of a four-volume set. Doubleday, Page and Company published it at Garden City, New York, in 1921. Braddy dedicated the volume to Blanche Colton Williams. Seven tales fill the contents. Frank Norris opens with The Ship That Saw a Ghost. W Clark Russell follows with A Nightmare of the Doldrums.

A tale of flight, The Kite, comes from Major-General E D Swinton. Donn Byrne's Superdirigible Gamma-I keeps the sky theme. Henryk Sienkiewicz's Lighthouse Keeper of Aspinwall turns back to the shore. Guy de Maupassant's Wreck and Edgar Allan Poe's Descent into the Maelstrom close the set. Norris's tale opens aboard the tramp freighter Glarus, off South America. The narrator hides his business there from the maritime lawyers.
62982-peter-parley-s-wonders-of-the-eart:
Peter Parley's Wonders of the Earth, Sea, and Sky is a nature book for the young. Wilson edited this new edition with additions and improvements throughout. Darton and Clark of London put the book out in its day. The work is given to George Birkbeck of the London Mechanics' Institution. Birkbeck's work to spread knowledge won the editor's warm respect there.

The preface scolds books that cram breadth into brief dry tables for children. Lists of genera and species can never teach sound method, he argues. Such tables leave the young mind disgusted or none the wiser. Mere memory work may be dropped safely as a direct aim, he holds. Keep the understanding active and the matter entertaining in form, he urges. Wonders of land, sea, and sky then draw the child on. A plate of the aurora borealis stands among the book's pictures.
6574-watchers-of-the-sky:
Alfred Noyes opens a verse trilogy on science with the watchers of the sky, from early star-gazers to the men who found laws in the heavens. His preface says the poem seeks the great moments when facts, long gathered, fell into a clear order, and changed how all folk thought. He does not try to cover all science, nor to build a new system in verse.

Instead, the torch passes from hand to hand through the years, each bearer adding light to the last. Noyes writes with a poet's eye for the human heat inside cold discovery, for doubt, toil, and sudden sight. Watchers of the Sky is a long poem about how star lore grew, step by step, into modern astronomy.
6612-myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-v:
Along the Rocky Range, Skinner follows the hope of El Dorado that drew Spaniards and later mountain men west. Gold finds in California and Colorado gave fresh color to that old dream, and tales of phantom trains, lost souls, desert riders, and a Yellowstone tragedy grew from it. The range itself looms large, harsh and grand.

Navajo arrivals, a goddess of salt, a flood at Santa Fe, and a battle in the air fill the later tales. Skinner writes with a westerner's relish for tall tales and hard truth mixed. This seventh volume suits readers who like mountain lore, where gold, gods, and ghosts share the same high trail.
6630-curiosities-of-the-sky:
Garrett Serviss invites readers to look up and wonder, with chapters on star-clouds, star-streams, and the passing of constellations. Windows of absolute night, fires in the heavens, whirling nebulae, sun banners, and the zodiacal light all get their turn. Comets, meteors, fire-balls, and the wrecking of the moon add drama to the sky.

Serviss writes for the curious, not just for astronomers, with pictures of nebulae, clusters, and the Pleiades to aid the eye. His tone is one of awe mixed with clear fact. Curiosities of the Sky is a charming, early popular astronomy book, still fun for stargazers today.
68482-mad-anthony-s-scouts-or-the-ranger:
Emerson Rodman wrote Mad Anthony Scouts, or the Rangers of Kentucky, issued in New York by Beadle and Adams. The tale was entered for copyright in eighteen seventy by Frank Starr and Company. Chapter one is Comrades of the Forest. A tall, spare backwoodsman sits by a smouldering camp fire. A genial faced Irishman in forest dress grasps his hand. Dialect talk opens the dime novel.

My name is Smith, Hezekiah Smith, says the backwoodsman, asking the other name. Pat Mulroony, lately from Tipperary, Ireland, the Irishman answers. He spied the smoke of the fire while travelling through the forest, he explains. A camp fire seen so openly meant either a green youngster or a band that did not care who saw it, he says. He knew Smith for a gentleman by his face, he adds. Kentucky rangers and Indian peril follow in Beadle swift style.
6904-boy-scouts-in-an-airship-or-the-war:
Ned Nestor and Jimmie McGraw, Boy Scouts of the Wolf Patrol in New York City, meet a Secret Service man named Gates in a San Francisco room. Gates has come from Washington to brief Ned, who has taken on a hard and risky mission for the government in South America. The boys at first take Gates for a poser, then learn to heed his warning hand.

The tale moves from city streets to camp and sky, as the scouts face spies in their own camp and danger from above. Ralphson keeps the pace brisk, with secret orders, strange warnings, and young heroes asked to act like men. It is a boys adventure of loyalty, pluck, and flight.
69215-touch-the-sky:
Alfred Coppel wrote Touch the Sky, a science fiction tale from Startling Stories in the summer of 1955. A midway sign offers a rocket ride twice around the universe for twenty-five cents at a fairground. Pete Moore smiles thinly at his wife Glory's giggle: in three days he flies a real silver ship from the desert.

Carousel music, popcorn tang, hot dog stink, ferris lights, and kewpie dolls crowd Pete's last night home on leave. He longs, homesick, for silent desert nights and cold blue air after too long away from cities and from Glory. Guilt and depression shadow the coming great adventure of flight. The tale weighs a test pilot's marriage.
70263-daughter-of-the-sky:
Paul Briand wrote a life of Amelia Earhart, issued in New York in 1960 by Duell, Sloan and Pearce. The book opens with Earhart's own poem on courage, first printed with leave of its holders. Briand thanks four books by or on Earhart, from the year 1932 to the year 1942, for leave to quote.

Three parts trace her path. A first flight as a guest made her famed, then she flew solo across the Atlantic and from Hawaii to California. School days in Kansas, work as a nurse's aide in Toronto, and a post at Purdue fill the gaps. The last part ends with her lost world flight and the search.
70638-ribbon-in-the-sky:
Murray Leinster wrote a space tale that ran in Astounding Science Fiction in June 1957, with pictures by van Dongen. An error is a denial of reality, but mistakes are mere mental malfunctionings, a quote from Fitzgerald's Practice of Thinking opens the tale. In an emergency a mistake may come from the need for precipitate action, it runs.

Most mistakes, however, are made without any such pressure. One accepts the first imagined solution to a problem without examining it. It turned out afterward that somebody had punched the wrong button in a computer. It was in a matter in which mistakes are not permissible, Leinster writes. But nothing can be done without a fallible human operating at some stage. A wrong button and a ship in peril drive the tale.
71237-exiles-of-the-sky:
Samuel Spewack tells of a pilot in Europe's young air lines in Exiles of the Sky. A prefatory note vouches for him: since the war he has worked as an American correspondent in Germany and Russia, and knows the scenes and the people. His pilot is Vladimir Uspensky, four years in the service without a crash.

The tale opens in Berlin's Tiergarten in sunless winter, minutes after the blow fell. The director drew a red pencil through Uspensky's name: no use for pilots who crash. Uspensky walks the park rehearsing his defense, two glasses of vodka and a leaking cooler, and the wound will not close.
71463-hanky-panky:
Hanky Panky is a book of conjuring tricks by the author of The Secret Out, edited by W. H. Cremer, Jun. Its subtitle promises very easy tricks and very difficult tricks. Diversions with dice, conjuring with cards, and jugglery with and without assistants stand in the scope. The tricks of gamblers stand exposed as well. The book holds 250 practical pictures.

It came out in London from John Camden Hotten of Piccadilly. A picture shows Robert-Houdin's famed rabbit trick, to produce a live rabbit from a man's coat collar. An opening note states the rise of the book. The Secret Out, a book of a thousand tricks in drawing-room magic, had a great success. That success led to this new edition of the same author's famed Hanky Panky, the note says. The work is a handbook of parlor magic.
76690-the-land-of-the-sky:
Christian Reid writes a tale of a summer trip in the southern hills in an Appleton volume from New York entered in 1875. Reid had written A Question of Honor, Valerie Aylmer, and Morton House before this book. The pages go with fond regard to the kind companions of a summer idling, the dedication states.

Eighteen chapters make up the tale, and a consultation forms an early plate in the set. Chapter one opens on a veranda at sunset with a family party in talk of a mountain trip. Eric warns that he does not advise the ladies to go, though he has praised the hills without pause. Aunt Markham fans herself in a large chair while Sylvia and Charley tease out his true wish to roam alone.
76944-dostoevsky:
André Gide wrote this study of Dostoevsky in French, first published in Paris in 1923, and Alfred Knopf issued the English translation in 1926. Arnold Bennett supplies the introduction. A saying of Nietzsche stands at the front: Dostoevsky was the only psychologist from whom he had anything to learn.

Bennett's note introduces Gide before Gide introduces the Russian. Gide, he writes, leads French literature: The Immoralist first made his name, and his tie to the Nouvelle Revue Française gives him unrivalled sway over young writers. His mark, Bennett argues, is a double interest, in the moral aspect of literature as much as in the beauty of it. Few critics match his curiosity about moral problems. Gide then turns that double lens on Dostoevsky, the novelist of crime, faith, and the underground man. English readers of 1926 got Russia's darkest novelist read by France's most searching critic.
77855-moussorgsky:
Montagu Nathan wrote a life of Moussorgsky for the Masters of Russian Music series, printed at London in 1916. Nathan had written A History of Russian Music. A portrait of the composer by Repin fronts the book. An introduction leads into four parts: career, Moussorgsky as operatic composer, choral and instrumental works, and songs. A list of principal works and an index close the volume.

Modeste Petrovich Moussorgsky was born on March 16, old style, 1839, at Karevo, a village in the Toropets district of the Pskof government. His father Pyotr was a small landowner, his mother a very fair pianist, and his brother was Filaret. The all important nurse completes the household picture. For her influence he was never tired of expressing his debt. Russian song and opera get their strangest master here.
a-son-of-the-gods-and-a-horseman-in-the-:
A Son of the Gods and A Horseman in the Sky gathers two Civil War stories by Ambrose Bierce, with an introduction by W C Morrow. Morrow stresses that Bierce was himself a boy soldier in the war, and calls these pieces studies of his many sided genius: poet, critic, satirist, and maker of fables. The volume appears as the fourth in a Western Classics series, with a frontispiece after a painting by Will Jenkins.

Each title names its scene. A horseman in the sky is a lookout posted above a valley, bound by duty to signal what he sees, even when the rider below is his own father. A son of the gods follows a young officer who rides out alone toward an enemy position to draw its fire. Bierce writes war as a test of nerve and obedience, with death close, plain, and rarely glorious.
boy-scouts-in-an-airship-or-the-warning-:
G. Harvey Ralphson's Boy Scouts in an Airship, or The Warning From the Sky, sends two Wolf Patrol scouts into a Secret Service adventure. Gates, a United States Secret Service man, enters a San Francisco hotel room with a warning hand raised, while Ned Nestor and Jimmie McGraw smile at what they take for detective posing.

Young Nestor has been engaged by the government for a hard and risky errand in South America, and Gates has come from Washington to post him on the details. From San Francisco the story moves toward airships, spies and the warning of the title. Ralphson writes briskly for boys, and readers who enjoy scouting tales mixed with early aviation and espionage will find it exciting.
britannica-1911-sandusky:
Sandusky is a city and port in Erie County, Ohio, on Sandusky Bay. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places it on an arm of Lake Erie west of Cleveland. Five rail lines, electric lines, and steamboats linked it to lake ports. A Carnegie library and a lake study lab were among its public features.

Trade in coal, lumber, stone, fish, and wine filled its harbor work. Johnson Island nearby held Confederate prisoners during the Civil War. Perry sailed from Put in Bay nearby for the Battle of Lake Erie in 1813. English traders came as early as 1749, and lasting settlement began in 1817.
britannica-1911-whisky:
Whisky, or whiskey, is a drinking spirit distilled from grain, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a long entry. The name most likely comes from a Celtic phrase meaning water of life, worn down first to usquebaugh and later to whisky. The usquebaugh of the sixteen and seventeen hundreds, though, was not modern whisky.

That older drink was a compound of plain spirit with saffron, nutmegs, sugar and other spices and flavourings. Grain liquor of some kind, though, has been made for many centuries in both Ireland and Scotland. The entry sorts whisky into three main types, Scotch, Irish and American. Scotch whisky splits again into pot still or malt whiskies, made from malted barley alone, and patent still or grain whiskies, made from a mix of grains. The malt group in turn has four main kinds, named for the Highlands, the Lowlands, Campbeltown and Islay.
britannica-1911-winchester-kentucky: Winchester is the subject of a short town article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Winchester is a town in Clark County in Kentucky, in the east of the Blue Grass region. It lies east of Lexington. By 1910 its people numbered over seven thousand. Three railways serve the town, one running toward the coal and timber lands of eastern Kentucky. The town holds a church college opened in 1866 and a trades school opened in 1900. It was first incorporated in 1792.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kentucky:
Kentucky, between the Ohio and Mississippi rivers, gets a full survey here, from its land and climate to its laws and church life. This entry opens with geography: the eastern mountains, the rolling Bluegrass country, the limestone plateau, and Mammoth Cave, described as the world's largest natural cavern. It then turns to people, wealth, farming, mining, and transport.

General history leads into religion, with a long section on how the Catholic Church grew in the state. Kentucky law touching faith is covered too. Rules cover marriage and divorce, the sale of drink, wills and charitable bequests, and cemeteries, which paid no tax unless run for profit. Sources cited run from early state histories to a centenary volume on Kentucky Catholicity from 1884.
charlemont-or-the-pride-of-the-village-a:
Charlemont, or the Pride of the Village, a tale of Kentucky by W Gilmore Simms, is dedicated to James Hall of Cincinnati as a pioneer of western letters. Simms's advertisement warns readers plainly: the domestic legend that follows is founded on actual events of comparatively recent occurrence in Kentucky. However strange the facts appear, and however they conflict with what is supposed of women's sensibilities, he insists they are unquestionably true.

The events behind the tale form the famous Kentucky tragedy. Anna Cook is courted by the brilliant Charlemont of the title. She is betrayed. Her husband Beauchampe avenges her, and Simms reserved Beauchampe's story for a sequel of that name. Village pride, seduction, and duel culture drive the plot. Simms, the South's leading romancer, treats the case as national material: proof that American soil grew passions as operatic as any in Walter Scott.
curiosities-of-the-sky:
Garrett P. Serviss's Curiosities of the Sky is a popular astronomy book that tours the wonders visible overhead. Serviss, a well-known explainer of the heavens, takes up star-clouds and clusters, the slow migration of stars, and exploding nebulae. He also covers the banners of the sun, the zodiacal light, the aurora, comets, meteors and the riddle of the asteroids.

Chapters also weigh the great Mars problem of his day, the wrecking of the moon, and the passing of the constellations as the heavens change over ages. Illustrations show the Andromeda nebula, the Milky Way, the Pleiades, the Orion nebula and the corona. Each marvel is grounded in what telescopes actually revealed. The book suits curious readers who want the night sky made vivid without mathematics.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NSRP-BereaKY_NS: A fragment of a news article covers a rally of the National States Rights Party in Berea, Kentucky. The rally was marked by violence. The article blames the violence on 'outside agitators,' a phrase officials used often in those years. The party was a segregationist organization, and Berea was a small college town. The publication that carried the article is not identified, and the fragment does not preserve its date or its full account.
in-old-kentucky:
Edward Marshall and Charles T. Dazey based In Old Kentucky on Dazey's play, issued in 1910. The tale is set in the bluegrass and the mountains. It opens with a girl singing as she rides an ox down Nebo Mountain. Sun, hair, and bare arms mark her as a mountain heroine.

She defies a stranger at a small bridge, saying no man can cross it. A father's murder and Lem Lindsay enter the charges she makes. Leaps over fire and fights fill the action. The book gives mountain honor and love in a stage-born story.
myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-volume:
Charles M. Skinner rides west along the Rocky Range in this volume. A phantom train on Marshall Pass opens the contents. Lost souls' rivers and riders of the desert follow. A Yellowstone tragedy and a Santa Fe flood raise the peril.

Over the Divide tells of men still hunting El Dorado. Gold in California and Colorado kept that old dream alive. Miners braved hunger, sickness, and death for treasure caves. Navajo tales and a goddess of salt add Native depth. Skinner's West is vast and haunted, where tall tales grow as big as the peaks themselves.
podcast-dannyjones-xXq5o5rW_kY:
Breath coach Will Grant teaches how to fix the body using breath in episode 50 of the KONCRETE podcast with Danny Jones. Grant argues that most people breathe badly and pay for it in stress, pain, and poor sleep. His fix costs nothing and starts with the next inhale.

Grant explains simple breathing patterns and the body systems they affect. He shows how breath can calm nerves, steady the heart, and aid recovery after hard training. Jones tries the methods and asks how to build them into a daily routine. Breathless and curious listeners alike get air treated as real medicine.
podcast-joerogan-5jKEYKrA4kY:
Rogan reacts, in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience, to the Biden administration delaying the release of JFK assassination files. By law, the records were due to open in full, and each delay has fed public doubt about what the files hold.

The talk asks why, six decades on, agencies still fight to keep pages sealed. Rogan weighs the official reasons against the suspicion that delay itself is the message. He places the fight in a longer story of government secrecy. For listeners drawn to the Kennedy case, the segment captures the mood of the disclosure fight as it stood then.
podcast-joerogan-uFiR3nVtYKY:
Music producer Rick Rubin sits with Joe Rogan for episode 1881 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Rubin co-founded Def Jam and produced landmark records across rap, rock, and country. He is famous for stripping songs down to what matters and for his calm, zen-like style.

Rubin talks about creativity as a way of paying attention rather than forcing results. He shares how he helps artists trust their taste and cut away the rest. Rogan asks about fame, failure, and making art that lasts. Makers of any kind get a quiet master class in doing less, but better.
the-adventures-of-prickly-porky: Thornton W. Burgess wrote The Adventures of Prickly Porky for his Bedtime Story-Books, with art by Harrison Cady, printed at Boston by Little, Brown, and Company in 1916. Chapters listed open with Happy Jack Squirrel's find and a stranger from the North, then Prickly Porky making friends, Peter Rabbit's startling news, Jimmy Skunk's call, and Reddy Fox in misery.
the-rise-of-david-levinsky: Abraham Cahan is named as author on the edition header. The header gives the title of his novel. It gives a September 2001 release date. A later update followed in March 2009. Only that edition header is present on these pages. Its general notices appear with it. No part of the novel itself appears here. Nothing about David's rise can be told from these pages alone.
the-young-trailers-a-story-of-early-kent: Joseph A. Altsheler's The Young Trailers, copyrighted in 1907, is shown here through its dedication and contents. Altsheler dedicates the Kentucky story to Sydney, a young Kentuckian. Twelve chapters lead into the unknown wilderness. A haunted forest, giant bones, and a wild turkey's gobble appear. The escape and the primitive man close the list shown. The story chapters themselves do not appear in the pages present in this record.
two-little-knights-of-kentucky:
Two Little Knights of Kentucky opens its contents with Two Tramps and a Bear, then a valentine party, a fire, and Jonesy's benefit. A dedication names nine children of the author's circle. No author is named on the pages shown.

Chapter one sets the coldest Saint Valentine's eve Kentucky had known in twenty years. Snow in Lloydsborough Valley shows every rabbit track, and an ice-cutter's wagon creaks up from a pond. Inside the depot waiting-room, a red-hot stove cannot clear the frost from the window-panes. Two boys run up the track with skates in hand, half an hour before the five o'clock train. The knights' adventures begin in that frozen station.
watchers-of-the-sky:
Alfred Noyes wrote Watchers of the Sky as the first volume of The Torch-Bearers, a trilogy in verse on the story of scientific discovery. His prefatory note calls the volume complete in itself. It finds an epic unity in that story: a single torch of purpose and endeavor, passed from hand to hand through the centuries. His poem treats the great moments of the work. After long labor, the pioneers saw their gathered facts fall into a significant order.

Those moments, Noyes says, hold intense human interest. They belong to the creative imagination of poetry. He does not try to cover the whole field, or to build a new system of science in verse. The prologue pictures a night among the stars, when the new hundred-inch telescope was first tried.
